note: The stars. Medieval astronomy held that they have no light of their own and shine with the light of the sun. Dante's Italian says that the one light shines in the many. So when the single voice of the eagle stops, the many souls blaze out in separate song.

context: It has just finished its roll of unjust Christian kings. Now it turns to the just ones.

note: The sound of a stringed instrument takes its pitch at the neck, where the fingers press the strings. The eagle's voice forms in the same way as it rises through its neck.

quote: The part of me that sees and endures the sun
note: The eye. Medieval books of beasts taught that the eagle alone can look straight at the sun. The eagle is seen in profile, so it shows one eye.

quote: He who shines in the center as my pupil
context: The Psalms were held to be inspired by the Holy Spirit, which makes David its singer. He brought the Ark of the Covenant to Jerusalem, dancing before it, a scene carved on the wall in Purgatorio 10.

note: A refrain. Each of the six portraits ends with what the soul has learned in Heaven, and in the Italian each of those stanzas opens with the same two words, ora conosce.

quote: the five who circle my brow
note: Five souls form the arch of the eyebrow around the pupil. They are named in order, starting from the beak.

context: The story of the widow, who stopped him as he rode out to war and won justice for her murdered son, is carved on the wall of Purgatorio 10.

quote: this sweet life and its opposite
note: Heaven and Hell. He has known both: he died a pagan and spent centuries below before he was saved, as the eagle goes on to explain.
Hezekiah, king of Judah. In the Bible, the prophet Isaiah told him he was about to die. He wept and prayed, and God gave him fifteen more years.
Prayer does not change God's mind. When a prayer seems to put off what was decreed, the delay and the prayer were both part of the decree from the start.

context: In 330 he moved the capital east to Byzantium, the Greek city renamed Constantinople, taking with him the laws and the eagle of Rome. That is how he "became Greek".

note: The Donation of Constantine. Constantine was believed to have handed Rome and the western empire to Pope Sylvester when he left for the east. Dante thought the gift well meant and ruinous, the root of the Church's wealth and worldly power. The document was shown to be a forgery in the 15th century.
William II, called the Good, Norman king of Sicily and southern Italy from 1166 to 1189. He was remembered as a just and generous ruler.

context: By 1300 William's old kingdom was split in two. Charles held Naples and the mainland, and Frederick of Aragon held Sicily. The eagle condemned both of them in Canto 19.

note: A minor figure in the Aeneid, killed in the fall of Troy. Virgil gives him barely two lines, calling him the most just of the Trojans. From that phrase alone Dante invents his salvation. Virgil's character is in Heaven, and Virgil is not.

quote: even his sight cannot reach the depths
note: The lesson of Canto 19 again: not even the blessed see to the bottom of God's grace.
A much admired simile. Readers have long compared it with a famous song about a lark by the troubadour Bernart de Ventadorn.
Dante is astonished. The eagle has just said that no one reaches Heaven without faith in Christ, and here are two pagans, a Trojan who died long before Christ and an emperor of pagan Rome.

quote: The Kingdom of Heaven suffers violence
note: Christ's words in the Gospel of Matthew. The eagle explains them: love and hope can overcome God's will, because God wills to be overcome by them.

quote: The first soul of the eyebrow and the fifth
note: Trajan and Ripheus.

quote: feet that would suffer and had suffered
note: The feet of Christ, nailed to the cross. Ripheus believed in a Christ still to come, and Trajan in a Christ already crucified.
Trajan. No soul in Hell can repent, so he could not be saved from there. He had to be brought back to life and given the chance to believe.

The prayers of Pope Gregory the Great, who died in 604. In a legend widely believed in the Middle Ages, Gregory was so moved by the story of Trajan and the widow that he prayed for the emperor's soul, and it was granted.
His second bodily death, this time as a Christian.
Ripheus. His conversion is Dante's own invention: a man so devoted to justice that God showed him, alone among his people, the redemption to come.
Faith, hope and charity, the three virtues that are God's gift. Dante saw them as three ladies dancing by the right wheel of Beatrice's chariot in Purgatorio 29. Having them, Ripheus needed no water.
By ancient reckoning Troy fell more than eleven hundred years before the birth of Christ.
God's choice, made outside time, of who will be saved. Its reasons lie in God himself, where no created mind can see the whole.

quote: do not yet know all the elect
note: Even the souls who see God do not know who else will be saved. People on earth have far less ground for deciding who is damned.

quote: whatever God wills, we also will
note: The same peace Piccarda described in Paradiso 3: the blessed want only what God wants, and that is their happiness.
Trajan and Ripheus, who flash together in time with the words about them.
